profile.reading:
Ark Data Centers' Duluth facility sits on Technology Drive near the intersection of Arrowhead Road and Rice Lake Road, a light industrial corridor north of downtown Duluth close to Duluth International Airport. The site opened in 2012 under the name Involta, an Iowa based data center company that chose the Duluth location deliberately for its climate and low disaster profile, citing an average temperature cool enough to allow free air cooling roughly eighty five percent of the year and distance from flight paths, rail lines, and other hazards colocation operators screen for. Local reporting at the time named Essentia Health as the facility's anchor tenant, with SISU Medical Solutions, CenturyLink, and Enventis among early clients, and identified Minnesota Power, the Allete owned utility serving the Duluth area, as the site's electric provider.

The company changed ownership and name over the following decade. Carlyle Group, the private equity firm, acquired Involta in late 2021, and the company relaunched under the Ark Data Centers name in May 2024, a rebrand its chief executive described as reflecting growth in infrastructure demand for space, power, and compute across a footprint that by then spanned six states, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Iowa, Minnesota, Idaho, and Arizona. Ark's own current materials describe the Duluth site as just over 26,000 square feet with about 10,000 square feet of conditioned data hall space and room for roughly 300 racks, a total facility power capacity of 1 megawatt, and a 1 megawatt N plus 1 diesel generator for backup, figures that are unusually well matched, meaning this is a facility designed to run close to its own utility ceiling rather than one built with large unused headroom. The company has also reported five consecutive years of ENERGY STAR certification as of 2023 and describes roughly a quarter of its local utility supply as renewable.

A 2026 Duluth News Tribune editorial, written amid a separate and much larger controversy over a proposed hyperscale data center campus in nearby Hermantown, described this facility as a small, well behaved, seventeen employee operation serving about thirty clients storing medical, financial, and research records, and used its long local track record as a counterpoint to fears about the newer, far larger proposal under debate. That editorial is a piece of community record about local sentiment, not a technical filing, and no county permit number, parcel identification, or assessed valuation for this site was located in this pass of research.

No precise street number found for Technology Drive location, description relies on Duluth News Tribune's "near Arrowhead and Rice Lake roads" framing rather than a confirmed civic address.

reading.body:
Ark Duluth is a 1 MW colocation facility opened in 2012 under the original name Involta, later acquired by Carlyle Group and rebranded as Ark Data Centers in 2024. The site occupies 26,000 square feet with roughly 10,000 square feet of conditioned data hall space designed to hold about 300 racks, and its 1 MW total facility power capacity is closely matched to a 1 MW N+1 diesel generator, indicating the facility is engineered to run near its utility ceiling with minimal headroom. The site was deliberately chosen for free air cooling available approximately eighty-five percent of the year and low disaster exposure relative to flight paths and rail lines.

At a conservative 3.3 kW per rack, the facility's 300-rack capacity would require roughly 1 MW of IT load, consuming the entire utility supply. This is not an AI training campus. The operator reports the site serves roughly thirty clients storing medical, financial, and research records, with early tenants including Essentia Health, SISU Medical Solutions, CenturyLink, and Enventis. The facility holds five consecutive years of ENERGY STAR certification as of 2023 and reports roughly a quarter of its local utility supply as renewable. No published certifications were found specifying hyperscale, high-density, or accelerator-capable infrastructure.

In Minnesota, Ark Duluth ranks second among only two facilities with published power figures, holding 10 percent of the state's disclosed 10 MW of total capacity, though the state has thirteen mapped facilities of unspecified size. The facility has operated without documented local controversy, with a 2026 local editorial explicitly citing its seventeen-employee operation and long track record as a point of contrast during debate over a much larger separate hyperscale proposal in nearby Hermantown. This campus does not represent material AI infrastructure capacity.
